column2: Troponin confirms myocardial necrosis and adds prognosis, but with ST elevation primary PCI is arranged on the ECG alone. Stress tests and CT angiography are for stable pain.
Every ACS patient gets aspirin (300 mg load, then 75 mg daily) plus a P2Y12 inhibitor. Amlodipine has no prognostic benefit and HbA1c 6.3% needs no extra drug.
Most MI deaths are early (often pre-hospital) from ventricular fibrillation; hence monitoring and rapid defibrillation. Cardiogenic shock dominates later in-hospital deaths.
Sharp positional pain with low-grade fever 1–3 days after a transmural MI is early post-infarct pericarditis; treat with aspirin. Dressler syndrome comes weeks later.
Prognosis after MI improves with DAPT, high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker (± MRA/SGLT2i if LVEF low). Amlodipine only relieves angina or lowers BP.
Load a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor/prasugrel) with aspirin before primary PCI. In inferior STEMI with hypotension, beta-blockers, diltiazem and nitrates can cause shock.
Rising troponin with dynamic ST depression is NSTEMI (high risk): angiography within 24 h. Immediate (< 2 h) only if unstable; CKD needs hydration, not delay.
In dissection give an IV beta-blocker (labetalol/esmolol) first: target HR < 60/min and SBP 100–120 mmHg. Vasodilators alone cause reflex tachycardia.
Sudden pale, cold, pulseless leg with sensory loss in AF is acute arterial (embolic) occlusion. DVT gives a warm swollen leg with pulses present.
Acute limb ischaemia: IV unfractionated heparin, analgesia and urgent vascular referral for embolectomy or thrombolysis. Long-term anticoagulation follows for AF.
Thrombolysis is harmful without ST elevation and is not given > 12 h after onset even for STEMI. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, fondaparinux and beta-blocker are all appropriate.
High HDL cholesterol is protective (reverse cholesterol transport). Hypertension, diabetes and high triglycerides are risk factors for coronary disease.
Unmodifiable risk factors: age, male sex and family history of premature CAD. Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, lipids and obesity are modifiable.
Persistent ST elevation weeks after MI with a dyskinetic apical impulse is LV aneurysm; echo confirms. Risks: heart failure, VT and mural thrombus.
Claudication (chronic PAD) causes absent pulses, cool hairless skin, pallor on elevation and rubor. Paralysis belongs to acute limb ischaemia (the 6 Ps).
Stable angina: exertional tightness lasting minutes, relieved by rest or GTN within ~5 min. Rest pain > 20 min suggests ACS.
Repair an AAA at ≥ 5.5 cm, growth > 1 cm/year or if symptomatic (NICE NG156). Aneurysms of 3.0–5.4 cm are kept under ultrasound surveillance.
Unstable angina has no necrosis; ECG is normal or shows ST depression/T inversion. Persistent ST elevation means STEMI and needs immediate reperfusion.
Hypotension, raised JVP, soft heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus days after MI is tamponade from free-wall rupture. A VSD would give a loud pansystolic murmur.
After MI with LVEF ≤ 40% plus heart failure or diabetes, add an MRA (eplerenone/spironolactone) to ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker; it reduces mortality.
Anterolateral STEMI: troponin confirms necrosis among the tests listed, but reperfusion never waits for it. CTPA is for suspected PE.
STEMI < 12 h needs immediate reperfusion: primary PCI if possible within 120 min of diagnosis, otherwise fibrinolysis. Antithrombotics alone do not open the artery.
Widened mediastinum with dysphagia and breathlessness from compression in a hypertensive man suggests thoracic aortic aneurysm; confirm with CT angiography.
Untreated thoracic aneurysms dissect or rupture; risk rises steeply above ~5.5 cm (the repair threshold, lower in Marfan). Tamponade follows dissection.
Every post-MI patient should take a beta-blocker unless contraindicated; bisoprolol is preferred if EF is reduced. Furosemide is only for congestion.
Predictable exertional pain relieved by rest with a normal ECG is stable angina: GTN, antianginal drug and CT coronary angiography. Unstable angina occurs at rest.
STEMI is diagnosed on a 12-lead ECG within 10 min: ST elevation in 2 contiguous leads or new LBBB. Troponin is not needed to start reperfusion.
GRACE (age, HR, SBP, creatinine, Killip, arrest, ST deviation, troponin) is the recommended ACS risk score. CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED are for AF.
If primary PCI cannot be done within 120 min, give fibrinolysis (tenecteplase) within 12 h, then transfer for angiography in 2–24 h (pharmaco-invasive).
In ischaemic cardiomyopathy with angina or viable myocardium, CABG improves survival (STICH) and treats the cause. Diuretics and ICDs do not.
JVP reflects right atrial pressure; recurrent PE causes pulmonary hypertension and RV strain, raising it. Dehydration lowers the JVP.
New harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with collapse 2–5 days after anterior MI is septal rupture (VSD). Papillary rupture gives an apical MR murmur.
Troponin may be normal early: a rise above the 99th centile with dynamic change on repeat (1–3 h hs-assay) supports MI. One normal test does not exclude it.
Primary-prevention ICD: LVEF ≤ 35% ≥ 40 days after MI on optimal therapy with good life expectancy. VF within 48 h of MI is reversible; heart block needs a pacemaker.
Smoking is the lifestyle factor most strongly linked to MI (roughly doubles risk, more in the young). Stopping halves the excess risk within a few years.
Fibrinolysis benefit falls steeply with time (best within 2–3 h, small after 12 h). PCI benefit is less time-dependent; aspirin and heparin are not.
Troponin I/T are structural myofibrillar proteins, highly cardiac-specific and raised for 7–14 days. CK, CK-MB, AST and LDH are less specific enzymes.
RCA occlusion gives inferior STEMI and, as it supplies the SA and AV nodes, bradycardia and AV block. ST elevation in I, aVL, V6 is circumflex territory.
Sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension after inferior MI is posteromedial papillary muscle rupture (single blood supply) with acute MR; echo, IABP, surgery.
Sudden pulseless collapse during acute ischaemia is most often VF; immediate defibrillation restores circulation. Free-wall rupture occurs days later.
Capillary refill < 2 s shows good distal perfusion. Coldness, pallor, hair loss and absent pulses mean advanced ischaemia; ABPI < 0.9 confirms PAD.
Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans): segmental arteritis in young heavy smokers with digital ischaemia and thrombophlebitis; only stopping smoking halts it.
Age is the strongest predictor of death after MI and weighs most in the GRACE score; prompt PCI after resuscitated VF carries a better outlook.
After large anterior MI, echo assesses LV function (guides ACEi, MRA, ICD) and detects apical thrombus needing anticoagulation. MRI best shows scar.
CABG gives the greatest survival benefit in left main disease and multivessel disease with LV dysfunction. One- or two-vessel disease with good LV gains symptoms only.
Late gadolinium-enhanced MRI shows scar and its transmural extent: > 50% transmural scar is unlikely to recover after revascularisation.
A peak aortic gradient of 25 mmHg is only mild AS. Recent ACS, recent stenting, severe LV dysfunction, insulin-treated diabetes and CKD raise perioperative risk.
Reaching Bruce stage 3 before ischaemia shows a high ischaemic threshold and low risk. Early ST depression or poor LV function means high risk.
Stopping smoking after MI cuts death and reinfarction by a third to a half, more than any single drug; aspirin, statin and ACE inhibitor add further benefit.
The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with anterior ST elevation and inferior reciprocal depression (anterior STEMI). Narrow QRS with P waves excludes VT.
